title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
A spatio-temporal point process — also called a space-time or spatial-temporal point process — is a random collection of points where each point represents the time and location of an event. Examples include the incidence of disease, sightings or births of a species, and the occurrence of fires, earthquakes, lightning strikes, tsunamis or volcanic eruptions.
The analysis of spatio-temporal point patterns is becoming increasingly necessary given the rapid emergence of geographically and temporally indexed data. This exercise combines several R packages to run a set of spatio-temporal point pattern analyses, using real-world forest fire events in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, Indonesia from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2023.

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Learning Outcome

The research questions
The specific questions to be answered are:

Are the locations of forest fire in Kepulauan Bangka Belitung spatially and spatio-temporally independent?
If the answer is NO, where and when do the observed forest fire locations tend to cluster?

text:
The Data
Two data sets are used:



Dataset
Description
Source




forestfires.csv
Locations of forest fires detected by the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor. Only fires within Kepulauan Bangka Belitung are used.
FIRMS


Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung
ESRI shapefile of the sub-district (kelurahan) boundaries of Kepulauan Bangka Belitung
Indonesia Geospatial portal









NoteHow this copy of the data differs from the textbook’s



The textbook’s files come from the Indonesia Geospatial portal and FIRMS’ authenticated archive. Neither is scriptable without an account, so the same two layers were rebuilt from open sources: the boundaries from GADM 4.1 at level 4, which is the kelurahan/desa level, and the fires from the FIRMS country archive for Indonesia 2023, clipped to the province.
The result is close but not identical, and the difference is worth stating:




This exercise

898
741


Eastern extent
108.85 E
106.85 E



The extent is the substantive difference. Belitung island lies between 107.5 E and 108.3 E, so the textbook’s boundary — despite the name Kepulauan Bangka Belitung — stops short of it and covers Bangka alone. Clipping to Bangka only gives 766 fires, which is much nearer the textbook’s 741; the remaining 132 fires are on Belitung.
The whole province is used here, since that is what the dataset is called and what the research question asks about. Every figure below therefore differs from the textbook’s, and the selected bandwidths differ with them.

text:
Importing and Preparing Study Area

Importing study area
The shapefile is imported, dissolved into a single outline with st_union(), stripped of its Z dimension, and reprojected to WGS 84 / UTM zone 48S (EPSG: 32748), the projected system appropriate for this part of Indonesia:

kbb_sf <- st_read(dsn = "data/rawdata",
                  layer = "Kepulauan_Bangka_Belitung") %>%
  st_union() %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748)

st_union() matters here. The observation window for a point pattern must be a single region, not a collection of several hundred sub-district polygons, so the boundaries are dissolved before conversion.


Converting to owin

kbb_owin <- as.owin(kbb_sf)

section: Importing and Preparing Forest Fire Data
text:
Importing and Preparing Forest Fire Data
The CSV carries longitude and latitude as ordinary columns, so st_as_sf() is used to build the geometry, declaring the coordinates as wgs84 before reprojecting to match the study area:

fire_sf <- read_csv("data/rawdata/forestfires.csv") %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
           crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32748)

A ppp object accepts only numeric or character values as marks, so the acquisition date is converted into three separate numeric and factor fields:

fire_sf <- fire_sf %>%
  mutate(DayofYear = yday(acq_date)) %>%
  mutate(Month_num = month(acq_date)) %>%
  mutate(Month_fac = month(acq_date,
                           label = TRUE,
                           abbr = FALSE))

title: Hands-on Exercise 3: Spatio-Temporal Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Visualising the Fire Points

Overall plot

tm_shape(kbb_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey60", lwd = 0.5) +
  tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "firebrick", fill_alpha = 0.6) +
  tm_title("Forest fire detections, Kepulauan Bangka Belitung, 2023")










Visualising geographic distribution of forest fires by month
tm_facets() splits the same map by the month factor, so the seasonal movement of the fires becomes visible:

tm_shape(kbb_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey70", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_shape(fire_sf) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.1, fill = "firebrick", fill_alpha = 0.6) +
  tm_facets_wrap(by = "Month_fac",
                 ncol = 4,
                 free.coords = FALSE,
                 drop.units = TRUE)

text:
Spatio-temporal Point Patterns Analysis: stpp Methods
This section uses functions of the stpp package to perform spatio-temporal point patterns analysis.

Preparing spatio-temporal point process object of stpp
Step 1: Extracting the forest fire coordinates from the fire point events.

coords <- st_coordinates(fire_sf)

Step 2: Creating a data frame by combining the x- and y-coordinates with the temporal event. The temporal event must be an integer.

fire_df <- data.frame(
  x = coords[, 1],
  y = coords[, 2],
  t = fire_sf$`DayofYear`)

Step 3: Creating the stpp spatio-temporal object with as.3dpoints().

fire_stpp <- as.3dpoints(fire_df)
class(fire_stpp)

[1] "stpp"



plot(fire_stpp)










Computing spatio-temporal K-function
STIKhat() computes the space-time inhomogeneous K-function:

kbb_stik <- STIKhat(fire_stpp)

plotK() visualises the output:

plotK(kbb_stik)



Guide to interpret the plot

If the contours show high values for small values of u and v, it suggests clustering at short spatial and temporal distances, meaning events occur close to each other in both space and time.
If the contours are flat or show low values, it indicates a more random distribution or a lack of significant clustering at those distances.

The spatial and temporal extent of clustering can be understood by observing how rapidly the contours increase or decrease along the axes — the spacing and values of the contour lines show at which distances clustering occurs.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2a: 1st Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Spatial Point Pattern Analysis evaluates the pattern or distribution of a set of points on a surface. The points may be the locations of events such as crimes, traffic accidents or disease onset, or of business services such as coffee shops and bus stops.
This exercise uses the spatstat package to discover the spatial point processes of childcare centres in Singapore. The questions driving the analysis are:

Are the childcare centres in Singapore randomly distributed across the country?
If not, where are the locations with a higher concentration of childcare centres?

text:
Geospatial Data Wrangling
spatstat does not work with sf objects. A point pattern must be a ppp object, which bundles the event coordinates together with an observation window (owin) describing the region within which the events could have occurred.

Converting sf data frames to ppp class

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(st_geometry(childcare_sf))
childcare_ppp

Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units








WarningPass the geometry, not the whole sf object



as.ppp(childcare_sf) also works, but it converts all sixteen attribute columns into marks and returns a marked point pattern. Two things then go wrong, neither of them loudly:

plot() stops drawing the points. Given a data frame of marks it draws one panel per mark column and prints the attribute values as text, producing an unreadable wall of overlapping labels instead of a map.
duplicated() compares marks as well as coordinates. Two centres at the same address with different names are then not counted as duplicates, and the check in the next section reports zero where the true figure is 187.

st_geometry() strips the attributes and yields an unmarked pattern, which is what every method in this exercise needs. None of them use the attributes.



plot(childcare_ppp)









summary(childcare_ppp)

Planar point pattern:  1925 points
Average intensity 2.417323e-06 points per square unit

*Pattern contains duplicated points*

Coordinates are given to 11 decimal places

Window: rectangle = [11810.03, 45404.24] x [25596.33, 49300.88] units
                    (33590 x 23700 units)
Window area = 796335000 square units



Handling duplicated points
Duplicates are a genuine problem rather than a formality. Much of point pattern theory assumes a simple point pattern, in which no two events share a location; where duplicates exist, several statistical methods either ignore the repeats or fail outright.

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp))

[1] TRUE


multiplicity() reports how many times each point is repeated, so the number of points involved can be counted:

sum(multiplicity(childcare_ppp) > 1)

[1] 338


The duplication is substantial: 187 points sit on a location already occupied, and 338 points are involved in a coincidence, so the 1925 centres occupy only 1738 distinct locations. Multiple centres registered at the same block or the same mall share one address point.
There are three ways to deal with duplicates. Deleting them is simplest but discards real centres. Attaching weights to the retained points keeps the information but complicates every subsequent analysis. Jittering — displacing each duplicate by a tiny random amount so that no two points coincide — keeps all the events and is the approach used here:

set.seed(1234)
childcare_ppp_jit <- rjitter(childcare_ppp,
                             retry = TRUE,
                             nsim = 1,
                             drop = TRUE)

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp_jit))

[1] FALSE


retry = TRUE makes the function try again if a displacement happens to land on another point, so the result is guaranteed duplicate-free.






WarningSeed the jitter, not just the envelopes



set.seed() is called before rjitter(), which the textbook does not do — it seeds only before the simulation envelopes. That is not enough, because rjitter() displaces every point by a random amount, not merely the duplicated ones. Without a seed, every re-render produces a slightly different pattern, and with it different Clark-Evans statistics, different selected bandwidths, and different G, F, K and L curves.
Rendering this document twice without the seed gave R = 0.55568 and then R = 0.55431 from identical code. The conclusions are unaffected at that magnitude, but any number quoted in the text stops matching the output beneath it. Hands-on Exercise 2b seeds the same call with the same value, so both documents work from the identical jittered pattern.





Creating owin object
An owin confines the analysis to the region where events could actually occur. Without one, spatstat uses the bounding box of the points, which for Singapore would include a large amount of sea and Malaysian territory — and density is events divided by area, so the wrong window gives the wrong answer everywhere.

sg_owin <- as.owin(mpsz_cl)
sg_owin

window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units



plot(sg_owin)










Combining point events object and owin object
Subsetting a ppp by an owin keeps only the events inside it and, more importantly, records that window as the pattern’s domain:

childcareSG_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[sg_owin]
childcareSG_ppp

Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2667.54, 55941.94] x [21448.47, 50256.33] units

section: Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
text:
Clark-Evans Test for Nearest Neighbour Analysis
The Clark-Evans test gives a single-number summary of whether the pattern is clustered, random or regular. It compares the observed mean nearest-neighbour distance against the value expected under complete spatial randomness (CSR).
The test statistic R is that ratio: R < 1 indicates clustering, R ≈ 1 randomness, and R > 1 regularity.
The hypotheses are:

H₀: the distribution of childcare services is randomly distributed.
H₁: the distribution of childcare services is not randomly distributed.

The null hypothesis is rejected if the p-value is smaller than 0.001.

Performing the Clark-Evans test without CSR

clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = "sg_owin",
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                nsim = 99)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.55207, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)








Warningnsim is silently ignored here



The header of that output reports a Z-test, not a Monte Carlo test, even though nsim = 99 was passed. The signature is
clarkevans.test(X, ..., correction, clipregion = NULL, alternative = ...,
                method = c("asymptotic", "MonteCarlo"), nsim = 999)
so method defaults to "asymptotic" and nsim does nothing unless method = "MonteCarlo" is set explicitly. No warning is raised. The clipregion argument is likewise inert with correction = "none", since it is only consulted by the guard-area correction.




Performing the Clark-Evans test with CSR
Asking for the simulated test gives the same R but a different p-value, because the asymptotic approximation is not reliable for a strongly clustered pattern:

set.seed(1234)
clarkevans.test(childcareSG_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                alternative = c("clustered"),
                method = "MonteCarlo",
                nsim = 999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Monte Carlo test based on 999 simulations of CSR with fixed n

data:  childcareSG_ppp
R = 0.55207, p-value = 0.001
alternative hypothesis: clustered (R < 1)


Both tests reject H₀. R = 0.552 is well below 1, so the childcare centres are clustered rather than randomly distributed across Singapore.






Note



The two p-values are not comparable at face value. The Z-test reports p < 2.2e-16, while the Monte Carlo test reports p = 0.001 — which is not weaker evidence but the smallest value 999 simulations can produce, since the p-value is (1 + number of simulations at least as extreme) / (1 + nsim). Not one of the 999 CSR simulations came close to the observed R. Increasing nsim would lower the floor; it would not change the conclusion.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2a: 1st Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Kernel Density Estimation Method
KDE estimates the intensity of the point process — the expected number of events per unit area — as a smooth surface, by centring a kernel function on each event and summing the contributions.
The single most consequential choice is the bandwidth (sigma), the width of that kernel. Too small and the surface degenerates into a spike at every event; too large and every local structure is smoothed away.

Working with automatic bandwidth selection method
density() accepts a bandwidth selection function in place of a number. bw.diggle() chooses the bandwidth by cross-validation, minimising a mean-square-error criterion:

kde_childcareSG_bw <- density(childcareSG_ppp,
                              sigma = bw.diggle,
                              edge = TRUE,
                              kernel = "gaussian")


plot(kde_childcareSG_bw)








edge = TRUE applies an edge correction. Without it, events near the coastline appear artificially sparse, because part of their kernel falls outside the window and is simply lost.
The chosen bandwidth can be retrieved directly:

bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp)

  sigma 
310.065 


Note the density values on the colour bar. The layer is in svy21, so the coordinate unit is the metre and the intensity is reported as events per square metre — numbers so small they are awkward to read.


Rescaling KDE values
rescale.ppp() converts the pattern to kilometres, which puts the intensity on a readable scale. This changes the units, not the geometry: the pattern is identical, only reported differently.

childcareSG_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcareSG_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcareSG_ppp.km

Planar point pattern: 1925 points
window: polygonal boundary
enclosing rectangle: [2.66754, 55.94194] x [21.44847, 50.25633] km


Re-running the same estimation on the rescaled pattern produces an identical surface with sensible numbers on the legend:

kde_childcareSG.bw <- density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                              sigma = bw.diggle,
                              edge = TRUE,
                              kernel = "gaussian")

plot(kde_childcareSG.bw)










Working with different automatic bandwidth methods
spatstat offers four selectors, and they do not agree:

c(bw.diggle = bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp.km),
  bw.CvL    = bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp.km),
  bw.ppl    = bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp.km))

bw.diggle    bw.CvL    bw.ppl 
0.3100650 4.4826926 0.4049553 



bw.scott(childcareSG_ppp.km)

 sigma.x  sigma.y 
2.159745 1.396370 








NoteWhich selector to use



bw.CvL returns a far larger bandwidth than the other two, and bw.scott returns one value per axis. Baddeley and colleagues recommend bw.ppl when the pattern consists predominantly of tight clusters, on the grounds that it tends to produce more sensible results in that case, while bw.diggle is preferable when the aim is to detect a single tight cluster against a sparse background.


Comparing the two most commonly used selectors side by side:

kde_childcareSG.ppl <- density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                               sigma = bw.ppl,
                               edge = TRUE,
                               kernel = "gaussian")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG.bw, main = "bw.diggle")
plot(kde_childcareSG.ppl, main = "bw.ppl")










Working with different kernel methods
The Gaussian kernel is the default, but not the only option. The kernel determines how an event’s influence decays with distance:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (k in c("gaussian", "epanechnikov", "quartic", "disc")) {
  plot(density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
               sigma = bw.ppl,
               edge = TRUE,
               kernel = k),
       main = k)
}








The four surfaces are strikingly similar. This is the standard finding in density estimation: the bandwidth matters a great deal, the kernel shape hardly at all.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2a: 1st Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Fixed and Adaptive KDE

Computing KDE by using fixed bandwidth
Instead of a selector, sigma can be given a number. Because the pattern was rescaled to kilometres, sigma = 0.6 means a 600-metre kernel:

kde_childcareSG_600 <- density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                               sigma = 0.6,
                               edge = TRUE,
                               kernel = "gaussian")

plot(kde_childcareSG_600, main = "Fixed bandwidth, sigma = 0.6 km")














Warning



This is where the earlier rescaling matters. Had the pattern stayed in metres, sigma = 0.6 would mean a 60-centimetre kernel and the surface would be meaningless. The number is always in the pattern’s current units.




Computing KDE by using adaptive bandwidth
A fixed bandwidth is a poor fit for Singapore, where density varies enormously between the city centre and the outlying areas. Adaptive estimation varies the bandwidth with the local intensity — narrow where events are dense, wide where they are sparse:

kde_childcareSG_adaptive <- adaptive.density(childcareSG_ppp.km,
                                             method = "kernel")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(kde_childcareSG.bw, main = "Fixed bandwidth")
plot(kde_childcareSG_adaptive, main = "Adaptive bandwidth")

Plotting Cartographic Quality KDE Map

Converting gridded output into raster
spatstat returns an im (pixel image) object, which base plot() renders but tmap cannot. terra::rast() converts it to a SpatRaster.
The unrescaled estimate is used here, not kde_childcareSG.bw:

kde_childcareSG_raster <- rast(kde_childcareSG_bw)
kde_childcareSG_raster

resolution  : 416.2063, 225.0614  (x, y)

Labelling that with EPSG:3414, whose unit is the metre, places the surface within 56 metres of the svy21 origin, roughly a thousandfold too small and nowhere near Singapore, so it will not overlay the subzone layer.
Rescaling is useful for reading intensity values off a legend, but the raster has to be built from the pattern in the units its CRS actually declares.




Assigning projection systems
The conversion carries the pixel values and the extent but not the coordinate reference system, which has to be assigned:

section: First Order SPPA at the Planning Area Level
text:
First Order SPPA at the Planning Area Level
A national density surface is dominated by the overall settlement pattern. Restricting the analysis to individual planning areas makes local differences visible.

Geospatial data wrangling

Extracting study area

pg <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "PUNGGOL")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")
ck <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
jw <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "JURONG WEST")


par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(st_geometry(pg), main = "Punggol")
plot(st_geometry(tm), main = "Tampines")
plot(st_geometry(ck), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(st_geometry(jw), main = "Jurong West")










Creating owin object

pg_owin <- as.owin(pg)
tm_owin <- as.owin(tm)
ck_owin <- as.owin(ck)
jw_owin <- as.owin(jw)



Combining point events object and owin object

childcare_pg_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[pg_owin]
childcare_tm_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[tm_owin]
childcare_ck_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[ck_owin]
childcare_jw_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[jw_owin]

Rescaling each to kilometres:

childcare_pg_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_pg_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_tm_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_tm_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_ck_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_ck_ppp, 1000, "km")
childcare_jw_ppp.km <- rescale.ppp(childcare_jw_ppp, 1000, "km")

The number of centres in each:

c(Punggol         = npoints(childcare_pg_ppp),
  Tampines        = npoints(childcare_tm_ppp),
  `Choa Chu Kang` = npoints(childcare_ck_ppp),
  `Jurong West`   = npoints(childcare_jw_ppp))

      Punggol      Tampines Choa Chu Kang   Jurong West 
           72           117            74           109 



par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(childcare_pg_ppp.km, main = "Punggol")
plot(childcare_tm_ppp.km, main = "Tampines")
plot(childcare_ck_ppp.km, main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(childcare_jw_ppp.km, main = "Jurong West")











Clark and Evans Test

Choa Chu Kang planning area

clarkevans.test(childcare_ck_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = NULL,
                alternative = c("two.sided"),
                nsim = 999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_ck_ppp
R = 0.86757, p-value = 0.0293
alternative hypothesis: two-sided




Tampines planning area

clarkevans.test(childcare_tm_ppp,
                correction = "none",
                clipregion = NULL,
                alternative = c("two.sided"),
                nsim = 999)


    Clark-Evans test
    No edge correction
    Z-test

data:  childcare_tm_ppp
R = 0.67866, p-value = 2.943e-11
alternative hypothesis: two-sided








NoteInterpretation



The two areas do not give the same answer.



Planning area
R
p
At α = 0.001




Choa Chu Kang
0.868
0.0293
fail to reject H₀


Tampines
0.679
2.9e-11
reject H₀ — clustered



Tampines is clearly clustered. Choa Chu Kang is the more interesting case: R = 0.868 is below 1, and at the conventional α = 0.05 the result would count as significant — but the threshold stated for this exercise is 0.001, and 0.0293 does not meet it. On the stated criterion the Choa Chu Kang pattern cannot be distinguished from complete spatial randomness.
Note also that these two calls use the default method = "asymptotic", so both are Z-tests and the nsim = 999 argument is doing nothing, exactly as in the national test above.








Note



The Clark-Evans statistic condenses the whole pattern into one number, so it says whether the pattern departs from randomness but not at what distance it does so. A pattern can be clustered at 200 m and regular at 2 km, and R will report only the net effect. That is precisely the limitation the Choa Chu Kang result runs into. Answering the distance question requires the summary functions — G, F, K and L — which are the subject of Hands-on Exercise 2b.





Computing KDE surfaces by planning area
bw.diggle is used throughout so the four surfaces are produced by the same rule, even though the bandwidth it selects differs from area to area:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(density(childcare_pg_ppp.km, sigma = bw.diggle,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Punggol")
plot(density(childcare_tm_ppp.km, sigma = bw.diggle,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Tampines")
plot(density(childcare_ck_ppp.km, sigma = bw.diggle,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(density(childcare_jw_ppp.km, sigma = bw.diggle,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Jurong West")








For a fair visual comparison, the same fixed bandwidth is applied to all four. A given colour then means the same intensity in every panel:

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(density(childcare_pg_ppp.km, sigma = 0.25,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Punggol")
plot(density(childcare_tm_ppp.km, sigma = 0.25,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Tampines")
plot(density(childcare_ck_ppp.km, sigma = 0.25,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(density(childcare_jw_ppp.km, sigma = 0.25,
             edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"), main = "Jurong West")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
In this hands-on exercise, I learn how to handle geospatial data in R using the sf package. Geospatial Data Science involves importing, wrangling, integrating, and processing geographically referenced datasets. By the end of this exercise, I am able to:

install and load sf and tidyverse packages into R environment,
import geospatial data using appropriate functions of sf package,
import aspatial data using readr package,
explore simple feature data frames using Base R and sf functions,
assign or transform coordinate systems using sf functions,
convert aspatial data into a sf data frame,
perform geoprocessing tasks using sf package,
perform data wrangling using dplyr, and
perform Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) using ggplot2.

Data Acquisition
The following datasets are used in this exercise:

Master Plan 2014 Subzone Boundary (Web) from data.gov.sg

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Getting Started
Two R packages are used in this exercise:

sf — for importing, managing, and processing geospatial data
tidyverse — for data science tasks including importing, wrangling, and visualising data

Within tidyverse, the following packages are specifically used: readr (importing csv), tidyr (manipulating data), dplyr (transforming data), and ggplot2 (visualising data).

pacman::p_load(sf, tidyverse)

plot() provides a quick way to visualise a sf object. By default, it produces a multi-plot of all attributes.

Working with Projection

Checking the coordinate system of a simple feature data frame

In that case, st_set_crs(mpsz, 3414) can be used to assign the correct label. However, this only changes the label and does not mathematically reproject the coordinates. If the data is truly in WGS84 (as with GeoJSON files from data.gov.sg), st_transform(crs = 3414) must be used instead.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1: Geospatial Data Science with R
text:
Geoprocessing with sf package

Use case 1: Land acquisition analysis

The scenario
The authority plans to upgrade existing cycling paths and needs to acquire 5 metres of reserved land on both sides of each path. The task is to determine the extent and total area of land to be acquired.


The solution
First, st_buffer() is used to compute 5-metre buffers around cycling paths. The cycling path data is first transformed to svy21:

buffer_cycling <- st_buffer(cyclingpath, dist = 5, nQuadSegs = 30)

Calculating the area of each buffer using the tidyverse approach:

buffer_cycling <- buffer_cycling %>%
  mutate(AREA = st_area(geometry))

Total land area to be acquired:

sum(buffer_cycling$AREA)

3687875 [m^2]


To visualise the buffer within a specific planning subzone (Tampines West), filter() is used to extract the subzone polygon, followed by st_intersection() to clip the buffers:

mpsz_selected <- mpsz %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")


buffer_cycling_selected <- st_intersection(buffer_cycling, mpsz_selected)













Use case 2: Number of pre-schools by planning subzone

The scenario
The authority requires a count of pre-schools in each planning subzone to support forward planning.


The solution
st_intersects() identifies which pre-schools fall within each planning subzone, and lengths() counts them:

mpsz$`PreSch Count` <- lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool))

Plotting the distribution of pre-school density using ggplot2:

       y = "Frequency")








Plotting the relationship between pre-school density and pre-school count:

       aes(y = `PreSch Count`,
           x = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`))) +
  geom_point(color = "black",

Getting Started

tmap — for thematic map creation

Importing Data into R

The Data
Two datasets are used:

Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) (GeoJSON) from data.gov.sg — geospatial data providing Singapore’s planning subzone boundaries based on URA Master Plan 2019.
Singapore Residents by Planning Area / Subzone, Age Group, Sex and Type of Dwelling, June 2024 (respopagesextod2024.csv) from Department of Statistics, Singapore — aspatial data with PA and SZ fields used to georeference to the subzone boundaries.



Importing Geospatial Data into R
st_read() is used to import the GeoJSON file, and the data is immediately transformed to the SVY21 projected coordinate system (EPSG: 3414). Unlike KML, the GeoJSON format already encodes attribute fields as proper columns, so no additional parsing is needed.

mpsz <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Only the first ten records are displayed by default because mpsz is a simple feature (sf) data frame, and sf objects print a limited number of rows to keep output manageable.


Importing Attribute Data into R
The population CSV file is imported using read_csv():

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv")



Data Preparation
A data table with 2024 values is prepared with the variables: PA, SZ, YOUNG, ECONOMY ACTIVE, AGED, TOTAL, and DEPENDENCY.

YOUNG: age groups 0–4 to 20–24
ECONOMY ACTIVE: age groups 25–29 to 60–64
AGED: age group 65 and above
TOTAL: all age groups
DEPENDENCY: ratio of (YOUNG + AGED) to ECONOMY ACTIVE


Data wrangling
pivot_wider() from tidyr and mutate(), filter(), group_by(), select() from dplyr are used. Column names are referenced explicitly in rowSums() instead of positional indices, as pivot_wider() sorts age group columns alphabetically (causing 5_to_9 to appear after 55_to_59), which makes positional indexing unreliable:

popdata2024 <- popdata %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG,
              values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`, `5_to_9`, `10_to_14`,
                                   `15_to_19`, `20_to_24`),
                         na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(select(., `25_to_29`, `30_to_34`,
                                              `35_to_39`, `40_to_44`,
                                              `45_to_49`, `50_to_54`,
                                              `55_to_59`, `60_to_64`),
                                    na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`AGED` = rowSums(select(., `65_to_69`, `70_to_74`, `75_to_79`,
                                    `80_to_84`, `85_to_89`, `90_and_over`),
                          na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`TOTAL` = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`:`90_and_over`),
                           na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(`DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`)



Joining attribute data and geospatial data
The PA and SZ values are converted to uppercase to match SUBZONE_N and PLN_AREA_N, and rows with no economy active population are removed:

popdata2024 <- popdata2024 %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ),
            .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)

left_join() joins the geospatial and attribute data using SUBZONE_N and SZ as the common identifier. Using mpsz as the left table ensures the output remains a simple feature data frame:

mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz, popdata2024,
                           by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ"))

Saving the joined data frame as an RDS file for future use:

dir.create("data/rds/", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")

text:
Choropleth Mapping with tmap
Two approaches are available for creating choropleth maps in tmap:

Quick plot using qtm()
Fully customisable map using tmap layer elements


Quick choropleth map with qtm()
qtm() provides a concise way to produce a standard choropleth map. tmap_mode("plot") sets the output to a static map:

tmap_mode("plot")
qtm(shp = mpsz_pop2024,
    fill = "DEPENDENCY")










Customisable choropleth map using tmap elements
For finer control over cartographic quality, tmap’s individual drawing elements are used:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.blues"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_title("Distribution of Dependency Ratio by planning subzone") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: Planning Sub-zone boundary from Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA)\n and Population data from Department of Statistics DOS",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))









Drawing a base map
tm_shape() defines the input data, and tm_polygons() draws the polygon layer with default styling (light gray fill, dark gray borders):

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons()










Choropleth map using tm_polygons()
Assigning a variable to fill within tm_polygons() produces a choropleth map. The default classification method is pretty and the default colour scheme is blues3:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY")










Using tm_fill() and tm_borders()
tm_polygons() is a wrapper of tm_fill() and tm_borders(). Using them separately provides more control. tm_fill() alone (no borders):

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY")








Adding borders with tm_borders():

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders()








Customising border appearance with col, lwd, and lty:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY") +
  tm_borders(col = "grey60",
             lwd = 0.1,
             lty = "dashed")











Data Classification Methods
tmap supports ten classification methods: fixed, sd, equal, pretty (default), quantile, kmeans, hclust, bclust, fisher, and jenks. The style argument in tm_scale_intervals() is used to specify the method.

Quantile classification (5 classes)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Equal interval classification (5 classes)

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "equal",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








The quantile method produces more evenly distributed class sizes compared to equal interval, which can be skewed by data distribution.


Custom break points
Descriptive statistics are checked first to inform break point choices:

summary(mpsz_pop2024$DEPENDENCY)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
 0.0000  0.6750  0.7283  0.7563  0.8140 10.0000      94 


Custom breaks are set at 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, and 0.90, with minimum 0 and maximum 1.00:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.60, 0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00))) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)











Colour Scheme

Using ColourBrewer palette
The values argument in tm_scale_intervals() accepts ColourBrewer palette names:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)








To reverse the colour direction, prefix the palette name with -:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)










Cartographic furniture
tm_compass(), tm_scalebar(), tm_grid(), and tm_credits() add map furniture:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5)) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))











Map Layout

Map legend
fill.legend and tm_legend() customise the legend position and title:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                title = "Dependency ratio")) +
  tm_pos_auto_in() +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_compass(type = "8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(lwd = 0.1, alpha = 0.2) +
  tm_credits("Source: data.gov.sg & singstat",
             position = c("left", "bottom"))










Map style
tmap_style() applies predefined layout themes. The natural style is used below:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 5,
                values = "-brewer.greens")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")








Resetting to the default white style:

tmap_style("white")

text:
Small Multiple Choropleth Maps
Small multiple maps (facet maps) place many maps side-by-side to show how spatial patterns change with respect to another variable. In tmap, they can be created three ways.

By assigning multiple values to an aesthetic argument
Assigning two variables to fill generates side-by-side choropleth maps:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = c("YOUNG", "AGED"),
    fill.legend = tm_legend(
      position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom")),
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
      style = "equal",
      n = 5,
      values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tmap_style("natural")










By arranging maps in a grid layout with tmap_arrange()
Individual maps are created separately and then arranged:

youngmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "YOUNG",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of young population")

agedmap <- tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "AGED",
              fill.legend = tm_legend(
                position = tm_pos_in("right", "bottom"),
                item.height = 0.8),
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
  tm_title("Distribution of aged population")

tmap_arrange(youngmap, agedmap, asp = 1, ncol = 2)










By defining a group-by variable in tm_facets()
tm_facets() splits the map by a categorical variable:

tm_shape(mpsz_pop2024) +
  tm_fill(fill = "DEPENDENCY",
          fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
            style = "quantile",
            values = "brewer.blues")) +
  tm_facets(by = "REGION_N",
            nrow = 2,
            ncol = 3,
            free.coords = TRUE,
            drop.units = TRUE) +
  tm_layout(legend.show = TRUE,
            title.position = c("center", "center"),
            title.size = 20) +
  tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5)

Creating Interactive Maps
tmap_mode("view") switches to interactive mode, allowing users to zoom, pan, and click on features for popup information.
Basic interactive map of the Central Region:

region_selected <- mpsz_pop2024 %>%
  filter(REGION_N == "CENTRAL REGION")
region_bbox <- st_bbox(region_selected)

stats <- boxplot.stats(region_selected$DEPENDENCY)
outlier_vals <- stats$out
outlier_sf <- region_selected[region_selected$DEPENDENCY %in% outlier_vals, ]

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name"       = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2)





tmap_mode("plot")

To prevent users from zooming too far out of the study area, set_zoom_limits restricts the zoom range:

tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(region_selected,
         bbox = region_bbox) +
  tm_fill("DEPENDENCY",
          id = "SUBZONE_N",
          popup.vars = c(
            "Name"       = "SUBZONE_N",
            "Dependency" = "DEPENDENCY")) +
  tm_borders() +
  tm_shape(outlier_sf) +
  tm_borders(col = "red", lwd = 2) +
  tm_view(set_zoom_limits = c(12, 14))





tmap_mode("plot")

Setting set_zoom_limits = c(12, 14) restricts how far users can zoom in (level 14) and out (level 12), keeping the focus on the Central Region throughout exploration.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2b: 2nd Order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis
text:
Hands-on Exercise 2a used first-order methods, which describe how the intensity of a point process varies across space — where events are dense and where they are sparse. Kernel density estimation answers “how many events per unit area, here?”
Second-order methods ask a different question: given the intensity, do events attract or repel one another, and at what distance? The Clark-Evans test at the end of the previous exercise condensed the whole pattern into a single number and so could not say. The four summary functions in this exercise — G, F, K, and L — are functions of distance, so they can.
The null hypothesis tested throughout is complete spatial randomness (CSR): the childcare centres are randomly distributed over the study area, following a homogeneous Poisson process. The significance level is 0.001.

text:
Data Import and Preparation
The cleaned subzone layer saved in the previous exercise is reused:

mpsz_cl <- read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")


childcare_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/ChildCareServices.geojson") %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%

Reading layer `CHILDCARE' from data source 
  `C:\Users\Imgigi\Desktop\629\hand-on-ex\hand-on-ex2\data\geospatial\ChildCareServices.geojson' 
  using driver `GeoJSON'
Simple feature collection with 1925 features and 16 fields
Geometry type: POINT
Dimension:     XY

Converting to a ppp and jittering the duplicates, exactly as in Hands-on Exercise 2a. st_geometry() is used so the pattern is unmarked; passing the whole sf object would turn the sixteen attribute columns into marks and stop duplicated() from seeing coincident locations. The summary functions below assume a simple point pattern, so removing the 187 duplicates is a precondition rather than a nicety:

childcare_ppp <- as.ppp(st_geometry(childcare_sf))

set.seed(1234)
childcare_ppp_jit <- rjitter(childcare_ppp,
                             retry = TRUE,
                             nsim = 1,
                             drop = TRUE)

any(duplicated(childcare_ppp_jit))

[1] FALSE



The two study areas
The analysis is run on two planning areas rather than the whole country. Second-order functions assume the process is homogeneous — that intensity is roughly constant across the window — and that assumption is untenable for Singapore as a whole, where the centre and the outlying areas differ by an order of magnitude. Within one planning area it is defensible:

ck <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "CHOA CHU KANG")
tm <- mpsz_cl %>% filter(PLN_AREA_N == "TAMPINES")

childcare_ck_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[as.owin(ck)]
childcare_tm_ppp <- childcare_ppp_jit[as.owin(tm)]

c(`Choa Chu Kang` = npoints(childcare_ck_ppp),
  Tampines        = npoints(childcare_tm_ppp))

Choa Chu Kang      Tampines 
           74           117 



par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(childcare_ck_ppp, main = "Choa Chu Kang")
plot(childcare_tm_ppp, main = "Tampines")














NoteReading a Monte Carlo envelope



Each function below is accompanied by an envelope() plot. The procedure simulates many point patterns under CSR, computes the same function on each, and shades the region between the pointwise minimum and maximum.
The interpretation is the same in every case: where the observed curve lies inside the grey envelope, the pattern is indistinguishable from randomness at that distance. Where it strays outside, CSR is rejected — and which side it exits on says whether the departure is clustering or regularity.
set.seed() is called before every envelope so the simulations are reproducible.

section: Analysing Spatial Point Process Using K-Function
text:
Analysing Spatial Point Process Using K-Function
G and F both look only at the nearest event, which throws away most of the pattern. Ripley’s K-function counts all events within distance r of each event, averaged over events and standardised by intensity. It therefore describes the pattern across the whole range of distances at once.
The plots below are drawn as K(d) - r rather than K(d) itself. Under CSR, K(r) = πr², and subtracting the expectation flattens that curve onto the horizontal axis, which makes departures far easier to see than a comparison of two rising curves.

Choa Chu Kang planning area

K_ck <- Kest(childcare_ck_ppp, correction = "Ripley")
plot(K_ck, . - r ~ r, ylab = "K(d)-r", xlab = "d(m)")

                     nsim = 99, rank = 1, glocal = TRUE)

NoteWhy glocal = TRUE and only 99 simulations



glocal = TRUE requests a global envelope. A pointwise envelope is a separate test at every distance, so with hundreds of distances some will fall outside by chance alone and the apparent significance is inflated. A global envelope has the stated coverage across the whole curve simultaneously, which is what a claim about the pattern actually requires.
The simulation count drops to 99 because K is far more expensive to compute than G — it counts every pair of events at every distance rather than one distance per event. With rank = 1 and 99 simulations the envelope is the pointwise extreme of those runs, giving a test at the 0.01 level.

text:
Analysing Spatial Point Process Using L-Function
K(r) grows as r², so its variance grows with distance too, and the envelope fans out at larger r even when nothing is happening. The L-function is the square-root transformation that removes this:
\[L(r) = \sqrt{\frac{K(r)}{\pi}}\]
Under CSR, L(r) = r, so plotting L(d) - r again flattens the expectation onto the horizontal axis — but now with roughly constant variance across the whole range, which makes the envelope width comparable at every distance. This is why L is normally the function reported.

Summary








Function
Measures from
Clustering shows as




G
each event to its nearest event
curve above the envelope


F
arbitrary locations to the nearest event
curve below the envelope


K
each event to all events within r
curve above the envelope


L
as K, variance-stabilised
curve above the envelope



The direction reverses for F because it measures empty space rather than proximity: a clustered pattern leaves larger gaps, so a randomly chosen location is further from the nearest event than CSR predicts. Reading F in the same direction as G therefore inverts the conclusion.
All four are global statistics: they characterise the pattern as a whole and cannot say where any clustering sits. That question requires local methods, so none of the four supports a claim about a particular part of the map.

Lesson 1 covers geospatial data models, coordinate systems, and thematic mapping with tmap. Importing, projecting, point-in-polygon counting, area normalisation, the age-group wrangling, and the standard choropleth workflow were all covered in Hands-on Exercise 1a and 1b, and are not taught again here.
This in-class exercise extends those methods to the parts the hands-on exercises do not reach:

confirming a spatial relationship statistically with ggstatsplot rather than describing it by eye,
building two analytical maps — a percentile map and a box map — whose class breaks are computed from the data distribution instead of chosen by a built-in style,
putting the same phenomenon into the raster data model with terra, the counterpart to the vector model used throughout Lesson 1.


pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, terra, tmap, ggstatsplot)

Two packages are new relative to the hands-on exercises. ggstatsplot extends ggplot2 plots with the results of the corresponding statistical test, so a chart and its confirmatory analysis are produced in a single call. terra is the current package for raster data in R, replacing the retired raster package.

section: Inputs Carried Over from Hands-on Exercise 1
text:
Inputs Carried Over from Hands-on Exercise 1
The two derived variables used below — pre-school density per subzone, and the dependency ratio — were both produced in Hands-on Exercise 1. The code is repeated here only so that this document runs on its own. The methods behind it are explained where they were first used: point-in-polygon counting and area normalisation in 1a, the age-group wrangling and the join in 1b.

mpsz19 <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSea.geojson",
                  quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

preschool <- st_read("data/geospatial/PreSchoolsLocation.geojson",
                     quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

mpsz19 <- mpsz19 %>%
  mutate(`PreSch Count` = lengths(st_intersects(mpsz19, preschool)),
         Area = units::drop_units(st_area(.)),
         `PreSch Density` = `PreSch Count` / Area * 1000000)


popdata2024 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respopagesextod2024.csv") %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, AG) %>%
  summarise(`POP` = sum(`Pop`), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = AG, values_from = POP) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`, `5_to_9`, `10_to_14`,
                                   `15_to_19`, `20_to_24`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `ECONOMY ACTIVE` = rowSums(select(., `25_to_29`, `30_to_34`,
                                              `35_to_39`, `40_to_44`,
                                              `45_to_49`, `50_to_54`,
                                              `55_to_59`, `60_to_64`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `AGED` = rowSums(select(., `65_to_69`, `70_to_74`, `75_to_79`,
                                    `80_to_84`, `85_to_89`, `90_and_over`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `TOTAL` = rowSums(select(., `0_to_4`:`90_and_over`), na.rm = TRUE),
         `DEPENDENCY` = (`YOUNG` + `AGED`) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`) %>%
  select(`PA`, `SZ`, `YOUNG`, `ECONOMY ACTIVE`, `AGED`, `TOTAL`, `DEPENDENCY`) %>%
  mutate_at(.vars = vars(PA, SZ), .funs = list(toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


mpsz_pop2024 <- left_join(mpsz19, popdata2024,
                          by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ")) %>%
  drop_na()

write_rds(mpsz_pop2024, "data/rds/mpsz_pop2024.rds")


nrow(mpsz_pop2024)

[1] 238








Warning94 subzones are dropped



drop_na() removes 94 of the 332 subzones, leaving 238. Checking column by column confirms these are exactly the rows where the population join found no match — no other column contributes an NA, so nothing is being discarded accidentally. They are the subzones with no resident population: the central water catchment, Tengah forest, the airport, the western industrial estates, and the offshore islands.
Two consequences follow, and both matter when reading the maps below. The white areas are not missing data in the usual sense but genuinely unpopulated land, so a dependency ratio is undefined there rather than merely unknown. And the sample size changes between sections: the correlation in the next section is computed over all 332 subzones, while the analytical maps are built from 238.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Analytical Maps and the Raster Data Model
text:
Statistical Analysis
The hands-on exercise plotted count against density with geom_point() and described the pattern by eye. Here the same relationship is examined with EDA and Confirmatory Data Analysis (CDA) together.
Geometry is dropped first, because ggscatterstats() expects an ordinary data frame:

mpsz19_df <- mpsz19 %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  mutate(`PreSch Density` = as.numeric(`PreSch Density`),
         `PreSch Count` = as.numeric(`PreSch Count`))

ggscatterstats() draws the scatterplot, the marginal distributions, the fitted line, and the result of a parametric correlation test in one call:

ggscatterstats(data = mpsz19_df,
               x = `PreSch Density`,
               y = `PreSch Count`,
               type = "parametric",
               label.var = SUBZONE_N,
               label.expression = `PreSch Count` > 40)














NoteInterpretation



The subtitle reports the Pearson correlation together with its confidence interval, p-value, and sample size, which turns the visual impression into a testable claim: r = 0.64, 95% CI [0.57, 0.70], p < 0.001, n = 332.
So the relationship is positive and clearly significant, but only moderate — density explains roughly 40% of the variance in count. That gap is the substantive finding, not noise: a large outlying subzone can hold many pre-schools while remaining sparse, and a small dense residential subzone can reach a high density on only a handful. Count and density are therefore not interchangeable, and the choice between them changes what a choropleth map of pre-school provision would show. The labelled points are the subzones with more than 40 pre-schools.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Analytical Maps and the Raster Data Model
text:
Analytical Map: Percentile Map
The classification methods available through style in tm_scale_intervals() all place the breaks automatically. An analytical map instead computes its own breaks, so that the classes carry a specific statistical meaning.
A percentile map is a quantile map with six fixed categories — 0–1%, 1–10%, 10–50%, 50–90%, 90–99%, 99–100% — obtained by passing an explicit vector of cumulative probabilities to quantile(). Both endpoints must be included.

The get.var() function
Extracts a variable from an sf data frame as a plain, unnamed vector.

arguments — vname: variable name as a quoted character; df: an sf data frame
returns — a vector of values with no column name


get.var <- function(vname, df) {
  v <- df[vname] %>%
    st_set_geometry(NULL)
  v <- unname(v[, 1])
  return(v)
}



The percentmap() function

percentmap <- function(vnam, df, legtitle = NA, mtitle = "Percentile Map") {

  # cumulative probabilities defining the six percentile classes
  percent <- c(0, .01, .1, .5, .9, .99, 1)

  # extract the variable and derive its percentile break points
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bperc <- quantile(var, percent)

  if (is.na(legtitle)) legtitle <- vnam

  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              breaks = bperc,
              values = "brewer.blues",
              labels = c("< 1%", "1% - 10%", "10% - 50%",
                         "50% - 90%", "90% - 99%", "> 99%")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle)
}







Notetmap v4 syntax



Lesson 1 and the earlier cohorts’ exercises use tmap v3, where breaks, palette, and labels are passed straight to tm_fill(). In tmap 4.x they belong to a scale specification handed to fill.scale, the legend title moves into tm_legend() via fill.legend, and the map title becomes a standalone tm_title() element instead of tm_layout(main.title =).

packageVersion("tmap")

[1] '4.2'





percentmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
           legtitle = "Dependency ratio",
           mtitle = "Percentile Map of Dependency Ratio")








The percentile map isolates the extremes a standard quantile map hides: the outer classes hold only the top and bottom 1% of subzones — three each, out of 238 — so genuinely unusual values stand out instead of being absorbed into a broad top class.

title: In-class Exercise 1: Analytical Maps and the Raster Data Model
text:
Analytical Map: Box Map
A box map is an augmented quartile map with two extra classes for outliers, using the fences of a boxplot as break points. Which value opens the sequence depends on whether outliers exist:

no lower outliers — the first break is the lower fence and the second is the minimum, so the first class is necessarily empty;
lower outliers present — the first break is the minimum and the second is the lower fence.

The upper end follows the same logic in reverse.

The boxbreaks() function

arguments — v: vector of observations; mult: multiplier for the IQR, default 1.5
returns — a vector of seven break points


boxbreaks <- function(v, mult = 1.5) {

  qv <- unname(quantile(v))

  iqr <- qv[4] - qv[2]
  upfence <- qv[4] + mult * iqr
  lofence <- qv[2] - mult * iqr

  # seven break points define the six box map classes
  bb <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = 7)

  if (lofence < qv[1]) {   # no lower outliers
    bb[1] <- lofence
    bb[2] <- floor(qv[1])
  } else {                 # lower outliers present
    bb[1] <- qv[1]
    bb[2] <- lofence
  }

  if (upfence > qv[5]) {   # no upper outliers
    bb[7] <- upfence
    bb[6] <- ceiling(qv[5])
  } else {                 # upper outliers present
    bb[6] <- upfence
    bb[7] <- qv[5]
  }

  # Q1, median and Q3 form the three interior breaks
  bb[3:5] <- qv[2:4]

  return(bb)
}

The breaks produced for the dependency ratio:

boxbreaks(get.var("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024))

[1]  0.0000000  0.4666279  0.6750233  0.7283114  0.8139535  1.0223488 10.0000000




The boxmap() function

arguments — vnam: variable name as a quoted character; df: an sf polygon layer; legtitle: legend title; mtitle: map title; mult: IQR multiplier
returns — a tmap element that plots the map


boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = NA,
                   mtitle = "Box Map",
                   mult = 1.5) {

  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var, mult)

  if (is.na(legtitle)) legtitle <- vnam

  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_fill(vnam,
            fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              breaks = bb,
              values = "brewer.blues",
              labels = c("Lower outlier",
                         "< 25%",
                         "25% - 50%",
                         "50% - 75%",
                         "> 75%",
                         "Upper outlier")),
            fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle)) +
    tm_borders() +
    tm_title(mtitle)
}



Static box map

boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
       legtitle = "Dependency ratio",
       mtitle = "Box Map of Dependency Ratio")














NoteInterpretation



The two outlier classes are what distinguish a box map from an ordinary quartile map, and both are populated here — of the 238 mapped subzones, 17 fall below the lower fence of 0.467 and 3 sit above the upper fence of 1.022.
The lower outliers are almost entirely city-centre subzones — Clarke Quay, City Hall, Boat Quay, Tanjong Pagar, Cecil — where the resident population is small and overwhelmingly working-age. The upper outliers are the opposite case, and Loyang West is the extreme: 500 aged residents against only 50 economy active, giving a dependency ratio of 10 against a median of 0.73.
That single value stretches the top class from 1.02 all the way to 10. An ordinary quartile map would have absorbed it into a “> 75%” class alongside subzones with a ratio of 0.9, whereas the box map separates it out as statistically exceptional.








WarningSmall denominators



SingStat rounds subzone populations to the nearest 10, so a ratio computed over a denominator of 50 residents is highly unstable — one rounding step moves it substantially. The most extreme values at both ends of this map sit in subzones with fewer than a few hundred residents, so they are better read as a signal to check the underlying counts than as a reliable measure of demographic structure.




Interactive box map
tmap_mode("view") switches to interactive rendering, and tm_basemap() places a reference tile layer underneath so the outlier subzones can be located on the ground. (The v3 guard tmap_options(check.and.fix = TRUE) is not needed — that option no longer exists in tmap 4.x, which validates geometries on its own.)

tmap_mode("view")

tm_basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas") +
boxmap("DEPENDENCY", mpsz_pop2024,
       legtitle = "Dependency ratio")







tmap_mode("plot")

tmap_mode() is a global setting, so it is reset to "plot" immediately afterwards to keep later chunks static.

section: The Raster Data Model with terra
text:
The Raster Data Model with terra
Everything so far has used the vector data model: pre-schools as discrete points, subzones as discrete polygons, each carrying its own attributes. Lesson 1 presents the raster model as the alternative — “cells organized in a matrix of rows and columns”, with the observed value encoded on the cell rather than attached to an object.
The lesson covers the raster model conceptually but works entirely in sf. This section closes that gap by putting the same phenomenon into both models, which is the clearest way to see what actually differs between them.

Building a raster template
vect() converts an sf object into terra’s own SpatVector class, and rast() builds an empty raster covering its extent. Only the geometry of the grid is defined at this point — cell size, extent, and CRS — not any values:

sg_grid <- rast(vect(mpsz19), resolution = 500)
sg_grid

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 69, 107, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 500, 500  (x, y)
extent      : 2667.538, 56167.54, 15748.72, 50248.72  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414) 


The printed header is the raster data model. size gives the matrix shape (69 rows x 107 columns x 1 layer = 7,383 cells), resolution the edge length of one cell in map units — 500 m, which is meaningful only because the layer is in svy21 and not in degrees — and extent the bounding box the matrix covers.






Note



Note what the header does not contain: any list of features. A vector layer stores an explicit record per object, so mpsz19 has 332 rows. A raster stores a value for every cell whether or not anything is there, so this grid has 7,383 slots regardless of how many pre-schools exist. That is the storage trade-off between the two models.




Rasterizing the pre-school points
rasterize() transfers the point layer onto the grid. fun = "length" makes each cell hold the number of points falling in it, and background = 0 writes a true zero into empty cells rather than NA — an important distinction, since “no pre-school here” is a measurement, while “outside Singapore” is not. mask() then sets everything beyond the coastline back to NA:

presch_rast <- rasterize(vect(preschool), sg_grid,
                         fun = "length",
                         background = 0) %>%
  mask(vect(mpsz19))

names(presch_rast) <- "PreSch Count"
presch_rast

class       : SpatRaster 
size        : 69, 107, 1  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
resolution  : 500, 500  (x, y)
extent      : 2667.538, 56167.54, 15748.72, 50248.72  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
coord. ref. : SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414) 
source(s)   : memory
name        : PreSch Count 
min value   :            0 
max value   :           16 


The header now carries min value and max value: no cell holds more than 16 pre-schools.
Checking that the conversion conserved the data — the cell counts must sum back to the original number of points:

c(points = nrow(preschool),
  raster_total = sum(values(presch_rast), na.rm = TRUE),
  occupied_cells = sum(values(presch_rast) > 0, na.rm = TRUE))

        points   raster_total occupied_cells 
          2290           2290            806 


All 2,290 pre-schools are accounted for, spread over 806 occupied cells out of 7,383.


Mapping the raster
tmap draws a SpatRaster with tm_raster(), the raster counterpart of tm_polygons(). The subzone boundaries are laid over it as a second tm_shape() layer for reference:

tm_shape(presch_rast) +
  tm_raster(col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
              style = "fixed",
              breaks = c(0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16),
              labels = c("0", "1", "2 - 3", "4 - 7", "8 - 16"),
              values = "brewer.yl_or_rd"),
            col.legend = tm_legend(
              title = "Pre-schools per cell")) +
  tm_shape(mpsz19) +
  tm_borders(col = "grey70", lwd = 0.4) +
  tm_title("Pre-school counts on a 500 m raster grid")














NoteInterpretation



The raster reveals structure the subzone choropleth cannot. Pre-schools trace the built-up corridors — the northern HDB towns, the Jurong and Tampines clusters, the belt running east from the centre — while the catchment, the western industrial land, and the offshore islands stay empty. Because every cell is the same size, colour here means the same thing everywhere on the map, which is not true of a choropleth over subzones of wildly differing area.
The cost is that the grid is an arbitrary imposition. Nothing in the world is 500 m square; change the resolution and both the pattern and the maximum count change with it. This is the modifiable areal unit problem, and the raster makes the analyst responsible for it, whereas with subzones the boundaries at least come from a real administrative decision.
